utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-01-48-T, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. This is a status conference. The purpose of this conference is to facilitate the proceedings of this case, and frankly speaking, this Bench was very disappointed and frustrated with no witnesses for the last week. I believe that we need an explanation from the part of the Defence. Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, thank you. The Defence apologises for the time lost. As concerns the witness who we were delaying about, he's now arrived in The Hague. I've seen him this morning. I've sent proofing notes through the e-mail which may or may not have reached the Chamber because they were only sent just before we came to court. He'll be ready to testify tomorrow. We do apologise for that -- for the procedure with him. As I indicated in a note I think that was circulated, we only became aware of his existence quite recently and it became apparent to us that he was a witness of potential importance. We did go to see him as quickly as we could and thereafter, the delays occurred in a somewhat unpredictable way following his health developments. He had a what might be described as a rolling series of appointments and the future course of those appointments was very hard to predict. At the time it looked like they would be limited and in the end they weren't. But he had the last of those yesterday and he's now arrived today. Now, it's an unsatisfactory situation and we are apologetic for it. I'm not sure how we could have handled that matter differently but in any event it happened the way it did and now he's ready to testify. As to other witnesses, the fact of the matter is that we have continued to cull the witness list down. There is a further development that I'm going to let the Tribunal know about soon. But the witnesses that now appear to remain are only four in number. Now, the witness that we have been talking about has instructed me today - and really only today did this matter arise - that he wants to make an application for protective measures. I'll have to provide some further details to the Prosecutors about that and see what their attitude is. I can deal with that straight away if you want me to, Your Honour, but it might be better to let the Prosecutors hear what we have to say and consider their position. I'm in the Tribunal's hands about that. That's why I'm not mentioning his name now. I'm sorry if I seem to be ponderous, but that's why. As to the other witnesses, Bahrudin Comor was listed for Thursday but he's not going to be called as a witness now. The Defence and Prosecution have held some discussions and a stipulation has been agreed on in respect of certain matters, particularly legal matters relating to the SVB. That will be filed with the Court in due course but the words have been agreed on. When they are, I'm going to raise a couple of other matters that go along with it and the Prosecutor will respond to those and we had in mind to do that tomorrow. But so that there will be a legal submission -- effectively an agreed fact or stipulation that will be filed with the Court. And having had those discussions with the Prosecution and having agreed on that the Defence is now not going to call Bahrudin Comor. He's been advised of that. That leaves Witness G who is to appear on Friday. We are advised that he will be appearing with counsel, and there will have to be further discussions with the Prosecutor as to how long that's going to take but I anticipate he's a very short witness. The other remaining witness on the live witness list was the witness who we indicated was present in Uzdol. Again, although he hasn't indicated as yet I see the possibility of a similar application being made. I'd prefer not to name him yet. We think the passport issue is to be resolved with him. We hope it's resolved today but as we understand his passport has been issued and it's on its way back to him so we expect and hope he'll be present on the weekend and ready to proceed next week on Monday. That would conclude the live evidence the Defence was proposing to call. There then remains the decision to be taken as to what to do with any witness that Your Honours refuse to allow us to proceed with 98 -- sorry, 92 bis. There may be witnesses that Your Honours say can't be dealt with that way and then we have to make a decision as to whether to call those. But as we understand some of those will be dealt with today and others will be dealt with soon. Again, we don't anticipate that that should cause major delays. And again, none of those witnesses, being 92 bis as they are, none of those witnesses seem to be central to the case although there are some in respect of which there is room for discussion and debate here. So for that's the position of the Defence case now, that -- we have lost some court time. I acknowledge and as I've said I apologise for it. I should say on behalf of the team that I'm lead counsel of that they really have, Your Honours, been working extremely long hours and endeavouring to avoid the sort of problems that have arisen and there has been a series of matters which have conspired to lead to these delays. However, although there have been delays, the delays have allowed for the Defence to further shorten its case so that in terms of completing this trial we hope that it will not compromise those matters. That's the report I can give you at this stage on the reasons why there were delays.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Although there is only four witnesses left, would you please be kind enough to submit a confidential list of the witnesses in the order that they are going to be called.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And as for the protective measures, what specific measures in your mind at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: With respect to the witness who would testify tomorrow --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We could go into the private session if you believe that we should.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes perhaps we should.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think those concluded the matters that I -- I'm sorry, Your Honours, I'm just receiving some static. Pardon me, my earphones were playing up. That concluded the 1 matter I was going to raise, Your Honours. I understand there are a number of matters Your Honours want to raise here. My learned friend is going to deal with I think the bulk of those. And at 5.00 I'm meaning to go back and deal with the witness once more and -- in respect of a couple of documents. But yes, those are the matters I wish to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you. And I believe there are some other matters we have to deal with that are mainly the procedural matters. If you have some previous appointment, you may withdraw at that time. I believe Mr. Mettraux is capable to deal with all those issues. Thank you. The next issue is about the 92 bis statements. The Defence filed a 92 bis motion confidentially on the 29th of June 2005. The Defence requests the admission of the statements of eight witnesses pursuant to Rule 92 bis of the Rules. The Prosecution response to the Defence motion was filed on the 5th of July 2005. After considering the arguments of the parties, the Trial Chamber will now render its decision. The Trial Chamber recalls the decision of the Appeals Chamber in Galic and has adopted the requirements set out therein. As concerns the first witness whose statement was filed in attachment A, the Prosecution has objected to the admission because parts of this statement would go to the acts and conduct of the accused as charged in the indictment. After careful consideration, the Trial Chamber does not agree with the Prosecution's position. The statement, including the parts of the statement challenged by the Prosecution, concern general information on the ABiH or information regarding acts and conducts of others than the accused. The Trial Chamber finds that the statement meets the requirements of Rule 92 bis. It's relevant and cumulative in nature and therefore it's admitted. The part of the statement concerning a letter by the accused sent to the Croatia press after the war is not an issue which would be pivotal to the Prosecution's case. The Trial Chamber sees no need to call this witness for cross-examination. As concerns the witness statement filed under attachment B, the Trial Chamber finds that the statement meets the requirements of Rule 92 bis as it does not go to the acts and conducts of the accused and is relevant and related to political and historical background. The statement is admitted. The Trial Chamber sees no need to call the witness to appear before this Trial Chamber for cross-examination. The admission of the statement of the witness which was filed under attachment C was not objected to by the Prosecution. The Trial Chamber finds that the statement meets the requirements of Rule 92 bis and the statement is relevant and cumulative in nature. The statement is admitted. The next is about the statement filed under attachment D. The Trial Chamber finds that parts of the statement challenged by the Prosecution do not go to the acts and conduct of the accused but, rather, relates to acts and conducts of others. Moreover, the statement is relevant and related to relevant historical and political background. The statement therefore is admitted. The Trial Chamber does not consider the evidence of this witness to be evidence which could be pivotal to the Prosecution's case and sees no need to call the witness for cross-examination. As for the statement filed under attachment E, the Prosecution has requested the witness provide oral testimony on certain paragraphs, submitting that these paragraphs go to the acts and conduct of the accused. Furthermore, the Prosecution has requested to cross-examine the witnesses -- the witness on other paragraphs, submitting that the evidence of the witness is pivotal to the Prosecution's case. The Trial Chamber will allow for cross-examination on the challenged paragraphs. The Trial Chamber will defer its decision on the admission of the statement until such time that the witness has been cross-examined on the statement. As for the statement filed under attachment F, the Trial Chamber finds that the statement does not go to acts and conduct of the accused as charged in the indictment. It's relevant and it's of cumulative nature. The statement is admitted. The Prosecution has submitted that it does not wish to cross-examine this witness. The Trial Chamber does not see a need to call this witness for cross-examination either. As for the statement filed under attachment G, the Trial Chamber found that the relevant parts of the statement have been read out in court during the testimony of a witness, that is Ramiz Delalic. As a result, the evidence contained in this statement is already part of the record. The evidence therefore is unnecessarily cumulative in nature and will not be admitted. The statement filed under attachment H, the Trial Chamber found the statement concerns evidence that does not go to the acts and conduct of the accused and is of a cumulative nature. Although the statement has already been discussed with the witness Delalic, the statement of 6 June 2005 clarifies a part of the statement of 17th May 2005. The statement is admitted. The Prosecution has not requested to be allowed to cross-examine this witness. Nor does the Trial Chamber see a need for cross-examination. It's so decided for the first group of the 92 bis witnesses. As we understand, the Prosecution will file their replies to the second group of the 92 bis witnesses very soon. Could I get some confirmation on this aspect, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We were hoping to file by the end of tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I've been reminded that for those documents admitted into the evidence, I would like to request the parties to ask for certification of these statements. I hope that we could deal with the next groups of witnesses within this week so that, to give the parties enough time to call those witnesses which need to be cross-examined since the Defence case is extremely short, for four witnesses I believe that we only need about a week's time. Yes, Mr. Morrissey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour I'll just say we are grateful to the Prosecution for hurrying up as they are and they were assisting hopefully were assisting each other but we were discussing the stipulations and I can say that Mr. Weiner made great efforts to meet with me and I'm grateful for him doing that. But we will respond very quickly when the Prosecution makes its response to the extents that we need to respond. We'll do that straight away. We don't need any extra time. If we were to get the Prosecution's response by Thursday -- by Thursday, we will reply on Friday morning. We would have a brief reply that we could make and we think it's realistic to do that. Your Honours, could I indicate I would be disappointed if we go as long as a week with what remains of the live evidence because the only witness for next week is the -- is the last witness, and I anticipate that his evidence would be a day but could go longer if the Prosecution have more to put to him but I think it's realistic to budget one day with him. So yes, Your Honours, we will do all we can to comply and thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Thank you very much. I only hope that the parties could take the extra effort to facilitate the proceedings of this case. Concerning of the motion for enforcement of court order re: electronic disclosure suite, this Bench have some problems or questions with the filing as well as with the reply by the Prosecution. So we may ask some questions to the parties. The Trial Chamber is seized by the motion for enforcement of court order re: electronic disclosure suite filed by the Defence on the 24th June 2005, seeking an order from the Trial Chamber for the enforcement of the May 7, 2004 order regarding the providing of an annex to the end, EDS, to the Defence, and to order the Prosecution to notify the Defence every time new documents are being placed in the Halilovic folder by the Prosecution with a short description of the material being placed therein. The Prosecution responds to the motion for the enforcement of court order re: electronic disclosure suit was filed on the 30th of June. Provision of the index as to who is -- seem to be not feasible but may be indexed as to Halilovic's folder. We are still not quite sure what kind of index the Prosecution or the Defence mentioned here. Yes, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon, Your Honour. We had the opportunity to describe the sort of index we had in mind, and we don't think it would be such a burdensome exercise for the Prosecution in the sense that the information we would expect is the information which we normally provided with when we receive disclosure under Rule 68 or under Rule 66(A), namely a very short, generally one-liner description of the document together with the ERN number of that document. Really the material that we need in order to be able to go through the EDS material is simply a document which would indicate to us very, very briefly whether there is any chance of relevant material to be found in each and every document. It doesn't have to be lengthy. It doesn't have to be particularly precise but it has to give us an idea of what is to be found in each of the documents. We had been given in the past by the Prosecution what they called at the time an index which was no more than the list of ERN numbers and those numbers means nothing for the Defence. We would have to open each and every one of the documents to find out ourselves what those documents contain. Furthermore, many of those documents would appear to be in the B/C/S language and neither counsel would be able to read those documents. So to answer Your Honour's question, the information which we would ask the Prosecution to provide would be a one-liner such as those one-liners which we have provided in relation to material which they have disclosed to us in the past. "Order of the 15th of January signed by Mr. Salko Gusic," for instance, or something to that effect which would avoid having to open each and every document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you still did not answer my question specifically. You mean all those documents in the Halilovic's folder or is it beyond that folder?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I must admit that we have some sympathy for the Prosecution difficulties. We are not suggesting that it's an easy exercise for the Prosecution either. We are simply submitting that it's easier for them than it is for us, and that there is a court order ordering them to provide us with search information. We would like to be reasonable in that regard. We think that whatever material would be relevant to us would or should be found in the Halilovic folder and at this stage we would only ask to be provided with an index in relation to that folder. If the Prosecution were to discover that material relevant to our case was misplaced or placed in another folder, I mean we would expect to receive notice of that fact. But at this stage we would only insist on the Halilovic folder being indexed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did the Prosecution already provide to the Defence such index and how this work and how many documents Halilovic's folder contains? Yes, who is in the position to answer that? Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll attempt to do so. The question Your Honour is asking is have we provided them with an index. Well, no, we can't. It doesn't exist. That's what we are trying to explain. When we put together a case -- the Prosecution in the letter which we annexed to our response to the motion, we explained there are over 4 million pages in our collections. There are many hundreds of thousands of documents relevant to the ABiH collections and what's loosely called the Bosnian government or Bosnian Muslim side. Now, to find any documents for a case such as this one - the Hadzihasanovic case, the Delic case, the Oric case - we have to go through different collections of documents. And when I say collections, I mean large numbers of documents which have either been provided to the Prosecution or seized by the Prosecution in a search warrant from various locations throughout the former Yugoslavia. They don't all exist in the same place. And they're catalogued whether they come in according to the collection they come from. For example, the Sarajevo collection, which is described in the EDS, is -- are those documents taken from a search of the ABiH archives in Sarajevo in October 2000. Some of those documents were used in the Hadzihasanovic case, some of them in the Delic case, some of them in this case. There are thousands of documents there. We analyse them by -- a language assistant looks at them to try to find relevant things. Investigator, criminal analysts, lawyers then go through and pick and choose those which are relevant and put them together as part of our case. But the remaining documents are just untranslated. They never will be translated. There are too many of them and they remain in that collection. Now, at the moment we have no way of indexing them for anyone to find them, us or the Defence. So what we do is we have something called an "IF," which is an information form which contains some information, and there is some metadata. Our evidence section at the moment is attempting to put together a system whereby an index might be available of some of the documents, maybe about half of them, but they can't do that before about September of this year. There will be no index before September of the documents in the 34 separate collections. We are in the same position as the Defence. Now, if documents go into the Halilovic one, it's exactly the same situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So you mean there is no special folder for Halilovic's case?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There is. There is. But I'm told it's empty. We have been -- my friends can correct me if I'm wrong -- we have been providing documents as we find them by CD or by paper disclosure, with indexes, list of index of what the documents are. So they have all the documents that we have used or we have decided are relevant. They have access to the entire OTP evidence collection with two exceptions, those are witness statements and Rule 70 material. In relation to witness statements and Rule 70 material we have searched those, we have put all the relevant search terms into those two collections and we have disclosed anything which is within Rule 66 or that we consider, and it has to be our assessment, within Rule 68. Those documents -- Rule 70 won't go on to the collection. The witness statements will when they are all redacted. That's going to take some time to do so. But in the meantime we are searching them. So we are providing the Defence with any documents that we finds in those two other collections. But in relation to the general collection, of the 70 per cent of the -- 70 per cent of our 4 million-plus documents, the Defence have the same access to those documents and the same search capabilities an as we do. Your Honour has seen at the trial the Defence have produced a number of documents that either the Prosecution did not have or did not find and there is an obvious reason for that: because the Defence is in a much better position to know where the documents are filed, where they are archived and what their relevance is than investigators working in another language. So the Defence actually have an advantage over the Prosecution in finding these. But there is a difference we want to emphasise between Halilovic-specific folder and the general collection which is where the documents are. We just can't index them in the sense of providing an index that you might find at the back of a book or the front of a brief. It's just not possible at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any way, I'm very surprised to hear there is no Halilovic case folder.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we will briefly respond to that. There is indeed a Halilovic folder which has three subfolders which contain documents. In addition to that, as my learned friend pointed out, we have access to a general collection. And one of the difficulties with the searches is that you cannot search both collections at once so you have to repeat your search every time. And as we pointed out in our motion, it has officially a 70 per cent retrieval power which is the official line. But our expert in the team, Mr. Cengic, has established I think beyond reasonable doubt that the retrieval power of this system is much lower than that and we have been unable to trace documents which we know to be in this system. Again, we are quite sympathetic to the Prosecution position but we would like to point out that Rule 68(ii) provides that it's for the Prosecution to provide us with an appropriate computer software to do those searches and at this stage the EDS system is anything but adequate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, let me consider this issue carefully and I believe that we have to hand out with the other judges and the -- we have to look into the practice of other Chambers on this matter. It seems to me that Mr. Mettraux, you are very familiar with the documents on the part of the Prosecution already. Yes. Well, just for the information of the parties, the decision on the admission of the Witness Karic's formal statement is filed today. The decision on Mr. Halilovic's 96 statement will be filed by tomorrow. The decision on the admission of the exhibits tendered from the bar table will be rendered by tomorrow. This is just for the information of the parties. Well, the next issue is about the planning of the trial. I believe at this stage the Prosecution has already received all the statements of the witnesses, including the 92 bis witnesses. Could I ask the Prosecution at this stage whether you are going to have some rebuttal procedure in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not clear at this time as to whether or not we would have any rebuttal. They are proofing their witness that is going to testify tomorrow today, and new proofing notes and more information can result. The witness that is scheduled for Friday, I don't believe we've received a -- we haven't received any proofing notes. I don't believe we've received any extensive statement, and I think everyone is waiting to or the Defence is waiting to meet with counsel and the witness. With regard to the witness that's coming on Monday, we have a -- not a proofing statement, a short, 65 ter summary or a 65 ter summary. We have the Prosecution interview but we are waiting for proofing notes. What I thought was going to be a very quick witness now there is an indication that it could be an all-day witness. So we don't know enough or we don't have enough information at this time to really advise the Court whether or not there would be a rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: When do you think you will be in a position to inform us whether there is any rebuttal?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When we receive more information and hear these people testify. We have -- the next -- after the one for tomorrow we have two witnesses that we have very little information. We really can't glean what they are going to testify to especially the one on Friday. We have no idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe you have received all the statement of those witnesses already so more or less you can see a roughly the picture of the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It's not really clear. For the witness for Friday we don't have a clear picture on what the witness is planning to testify to. With regard to Monday we have some idea and tomorrow, but I spoke to counsel this morning and I said, did the witness for tomorrow bring documents with him or her? And they were uncertain at that time. And this was in the morning so I'm not clear whether or not that person has brought any documents. Will the witness for Friday bring any documents? Unclear. Monday? Unclear. Until we get an idea of what if anything they are going to be producing and what if anything they will be saying we really can't answer that. I would surmise there would be very little if any rebuttal, but I would not close the door to that until we really hear them or get some more information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe next Monday, you are in a better position to inform us about your decision concerning rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, let's set next Monday for the date that we will get more concrete information about the positions on the Prosecution concerning of the rebuttal. We hope that we could have the rebuttal procedure, if there is any, before the summer recess. So tentatively, tentatively, at this stage, I hope the parties could file their final brief by Tuesday, 16th August, right after the summer recess. And if possible, we will have the final arguments next week; that is, on the 22nd of August. This is a very tentative schedule. I just want to warn the parties to be prepared for that date. Are there any other matters that the parties would like to raise at this stage? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, very briefly. The first one concerned the Defence exhibits. Because the Defence has decided to call such a limited number of witnesses, we are going to be left with a number of documents which we would like to tender and what we are proposing to do is we have asked the Prosecution to consider the binder of documents which we intend to seek to tender and which we also provided to Chamber, for them to consider whether they have any objection to any of those documents, and if so, to which one. If to none, we would seek to tender those by agreement. There is also the possibility of the Defence making a brief and very short motion to amend its Rule 65 ter of exhibits. We've received a number of new documents in the past week or two and we have also received a number of translations from CLSS of documents which neither counsel had been able to read and it may be that we may be able to file a short motion, either at the end of this week but probably at the beginning of the next when we've received all translation to amend our Rule 65 ter. We would think that it would relate to 10 or 12 new documents, and again we with would provide copies immediately to the Prosecution to see whether they would have any objection to that tendering. Yes. We've also sought now to cut the list even further than the list which appeared at the front page of the binder which we provided to the Defence and -- to the Chamber and to the Prosecution and we will discuss that matter even further with the Prosecution, but we anticipate that there is going to be only very few documents that we will seek to tender. The second issue which I would like to address very briefly is an application for provisional release which the Defence will be making tomorrow, for the provisional release of Mr. Halilovic between the time of the end of the trial until that time when judgement in this case is rendered and/or the time for final argument. So this motion will be filed first thing tomorrow morning. Actually it's been provided to the Registry already. Third matter briefly is the issue of Rule 65 -- Rule 68 disclosure. We would like to place it on the record at this stage that this is the Defence understanding, that a full and complete Rule 68 search of existing Prosecution material has been conducted. Experience taught us, at least in this Tribunal, that a number of documents suddenly appear in proceedings when the matter goes on appeal and we would like to make sure that if there is an appeal in this case this doesn't happen. We would just like to place that this is our understanding at this stage, that all of the material in possession of the Prosecution has been going through carefully Rule 68 search. The last two matters, Your Honour, is concerning a number of letters which the Defence has sent to the Prosecution and for which there has been no responses. At this stage, we will await those responses and hope that they will be coming before the end of our case. If that were not to be the case we reserve our right to ask the Trial Chamber to draw a number of inferences from this failure. Finally, and lastly, the issue of cross-examination material. There is a court order to the effect that cross-examination material should be provided to the Defence, I believe the words of the court are "as soon as possible." We would just like to indicate that we have received none so far and we would be grateful to receive that material both for the witness tomorrow but also if possible for the witness for Friday to receive that material if possible today. That's all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. As for the first issue, that a -- I believe that there is various ways for the parties to tender their documents. Maybe when we render our decision concerning the documents tendered through the bar table, that will be helpful also to the Defence case. As for the provisional release, as I said that we are expecting the parties to file their final briefs on the 16th of August and final argument will be heard on Monday, 22nd August. So at that time the Bench will consider the request of the provisional release but not before, because we had a very tight schedule at our hands. And I also hope Mr. Halilovic will be present during the final argument. Well, as for the 68 disclosure, I believe Mr. Mettraux has said what he wanted to say and it is in the record already. I understand so long as the case is going on, the 68 -- Rule 68 matters will be with us. As for the last matter, about material in the cross-examination, it is true that the Bench made a decision and we delivered several oral decisions concerning of this matter, and I hope that the parties could treat this matter with the attitude of bona fide so as to facilitate the proceedings of this trial. Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just with respect to that last matter, I can indicate that I think Mr. Re is proceeding with bona fides, he spoke to me today. We have arranged in relation to tomorrow's witness that he will give me such material tonight. I happen to know the Prosecution have got a number of pressures on them and we appreciate that in the real world, that in respect of this witness there is no doubt that he's made the relevant efforts and that he's going to give me what I need tonight. I think that's an example of what Your Honour refers to. We have no suspicion about that. As long as I get it tonight, with respect to this particular witness I'm happy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It's very encouraging. Are there any other matters on the parts of the Prosecution? Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, other than just in response to the request for Rule 68, for the Court to please be advised and for the record that Rule 68 is ongoing, that whenever we receive a list of witnesses, we make checks on those witnesses. When witnesses are definitely on the list, we run checks on those and if there is anything that is Rule 68, it's provided. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Morrissey? No? Well, I believe that's all for today's status conference, and I'm looking forward to see you tomorrow for the next witness. The hearing for this afternoon is adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.01 p.m.
